overview: This atlas label spans 2000 BCE to 1279 CE across parts of Alaska, Arctic Canada, Greenland and later Siberia. It gathers distinct archaeological communities under a broad description of livelihood. Saqqaq, Dorset and later maritime traditions had different histories; the shading identifies neither a single kingdom nor one unchanging people.

periods.title: Earlier regional communities
periods.summary: Saqqaq communities already occupied Greenland before the map begins; their approximately 2500 to 800 BCE chronology is regional.

periods.title: Different traditions in different regions
periods.summary: Dorset communities in the eastern Arctic and Old Bering Sea craftspeople in Alaska belong to distinct regional histories.

periods.title: Thule migrations and regional change
periods.summary: New radiocarbon dates at two western Canadian sites support thirteenth-century Thule migration; the exact timing remains debated.

items.text: The outline is coarse: it omits Qeqertasussuk in Disko Bay and Cape Espenberg in Alaska, while Qajartalik is included in an earlier snapshot but excluded by 1200. These named places provide comparative regional evidence, not proof that every settlement belongs inside every shaded boundary. Separate Dorset, Thule and Inuit map records retain their own scope.

Permafrost at Saqqaq sites preserved wood, bone, antler, ivory and skin that usually decay. These finds reveal skilled makers working in many materials. A landscape that looks almost treeless could still supply driftwood, carried there from elsewhere and used for tools and fuel.

Qeqertasussuk’s frozen refuse contained remains of 45 vertebrate species, plus molluscs and traces of berries. Seals mattered, but so did fish, birds and land animals. The ancient menu was much more varied than the atlas label suggests: even a marine hunter could appreciate a berry.

Jens Fog Jensen’s Disko Bay research identifies likely single-family summer tents among both Saqqaq and Dorset remains. Some had a central hearth; others had parallel stone rows dividing the interior. Families could move between larger resource-rich settlements and smaller seasonal camps. Moving house sometimes meant carrying the house.

Some Dorset winter dwellings in that regional study had two platforms beside a central floor. Multiple hearths or lamp stands, with similar tool distributions on opposite sides, suggest two households sharing the building. The stones preserve a possible household arrangement, although they cannot tell us everyone’s name or exact relationship.

Stone supplies also shaped journeys. Jensen found that hunting parties probably collected killiaq stone at Angissat during summer trips. At Qaarsut, workers prepared rough tool shapes for distribution across western Greenland. Gathering food and obtaining material for the next set of tools could be parts of the same journey.

In Early Dorset Disko Bay, animal resources supplied clothing hides as well as food, bone, antler and ivory. Craftspeople carved soapstone lamps and made tiny cutting blades from carefully chosen minerals. Locally available quartz and stones brought from farther away served different tasks: the household toolkit was a collection of material knowledge.

A North Baffin carving tool in the Canadian Museum of History is only about 13 centimetres long. Its description explains a clever fitting: pressing a bone insert tightened the blade in its wooden handle. It appears in the museum’s Dorset discussion, although its formal cultural-affiliation field remains unresolved.

At Birnirk near Utqiagvik, square houses were roughly 12 feet across, with driftwood and whalebone frames under sod roofs. Their entrances lay below the plank floors to help retain warmth. A low doorway was useful engineering in a cold climate, even if it made coming home less upright than usual.

Birnirk’s mounds grew as people rebuilt over older homes. The site may have held only two or three occupied houses at a time, despite the many surviving mounds. Stone lamps provided light and heat. The whole archaeological landscape represents repeated lives, not a snapshot of one crowded village.

Remains of an approximately thousand-year-old umiak survived at Birnirk, including decorative ivory inlays and baleen lashings. Such preservation is rare for a boat made from organic materials. It reveals both the practical skill of joining components and a wish to make useful equipment visually distinctive.

Where did coastal builders find logs? Alix and Mason describe trees carried down rivers such as the Yukon and Kuskokwim, then moved by currents, wind and sea ice. Spruce, cottonwood and willow reached Arctic shores this way. The sea could deliver building materials as well as food.

The earliest excavated houses in Cape Espenberg’s eleventh- to eighteenth-century sequence used large logs, often unsplit, with split wood for floors or benches. Posts supported stacked horizontal walls. Preserved wood shows deliberate construction choices; the region’s builders were carpenters, not simply people sheltering beneath whatever washed ashore.

An Alaskan harpoon counterweight dated 300 to 500 CE, classified as Old Bering Sea III, combines engineering and ornament. Carved from walrus ivory, it helped stabilize a hunting weapon. Its curved engraved designs are visible evidence of artistry; the museum cautiously suggests that some features may represent animals.

sections.title: Sounds, images and learning about the past

items.text: A wooden drum rim from North Baffin is catalogued as Dorset. Its outside diameter is about 17 centimetres. The museum suggests drums of this kind may have accompanied dances or ceremonies, by comparison with later Inuit use. The instrument survives; its rhythm, songs and exact occasions do not.

At Qajartalik in Nunavik, roughly 180 human or human-like faces were carved into soapstone. Engraved outlines enclose eyes, noses and mouths. The museum attributes them to Dorset makers, associated with Tuniit in Inuit oral histories, and tentatively estimates their age at 1500 to 750 years through comparison with other sites.

These faces supply an authentic visual record, not a securely translated written sentence. Their intended audience and meaning remain questions. In 2022, museum researchers worked with Avataq, Makivik and Kangiqsujuaq partners to scan the site in three dimensions, including how changing light affects the faces. Learning about this past is collaborative work.

Arctic chronology changes with new evidence. Friesen and Arnold’s 2008 study dated early Thule settlements at Nelson River and Washout to the thirteenth century, supporting a later eastward migration than the often-repeated date of 1000 CE. This is an argument from particular sites, not a calendar for every northern community.

A separate study reported 56 radiocarbon dates from three Late Dorset sites near Iqaluktuuq on Victoria Island. They showed settlement continuing after 1300, beyond this card’s endpoint. Dorset and Thule occupation therefore overlapped in neighbouring regions; the evidence does not establish that particular families met.

ending.text: The map stops in 1279, but Arctic life did not. Regional traditions changed, and living Indigenous communities continue to make their own histories. Founded in 1977, the Inuit Circumpolar Council represents Inuit across Alaska, Canada, Kalaallit Nunaat and Chukotka. That modern organization is not an ancient government or proof that every earlier archaeological group had one shared identity.
